title: Why Brushing Your Child's Teeth Is Not Enough to Prevent Cavities
body: Today's children face a higher risk of tooth decay than in previous generations, and diet is a big, often-overlooked reason why. The post cites Parents Magazine's estimate that at least 4 million preschoolers have tooth decay, an increase of more than 600,000 kids over the prior decade, and notes CDC data reported by USA Today that tooth decay is the most common childhood disease -- roughly five times as common as asthma and seven times as common as hay fever.
Diets high in sugar, carbohydrates, and sweets raise a child's cavity risk from an early age, so the post argues that brushing alone isn't enough without also managing what kids eat.

Practical prevention tips: favor snacks that dissolve easily over sticky ones that linger on teeth for hours; avoid sweet, sticky, or starchy snacks between meals to limit plaque buildup; and save 'fun foods' for special occasions so kids develop a taste for balanced meals over time.
Safe snack examples given: cheese, fresh fruit, vegetables, yogurt, nuts, plain milk, rice cakes, Cheerios, crackers, and oatmeal.
Snacks to limit: dried fruit, chewy fruit snacks, sweetened juice, soda, chips, sticky candy, cakes, cookies, sports drinks, chewy granola bars, sugary cereal, and flavored milk.
The post suggests hard chewable vitamins or vitamin drops instead of gummy vitamins, given after dinner so teeth can be brushed and flossed shortly after.

It also warns that 'sugar-free' or 'sugarless' labels can be misleading, since products may still contain other sugars in disguise -- listing corn syrup, fructose, corn sugar, malt, glucose, maltose, corn sweetener, high fructose, sorbitol, and lactose as ingredients to watch for.

The post closes by framing tooth decay as preventable through diet monitoring, noting that good nutrition habits also help guard against diabetes and obesity, and invites readers to schedule a cleaning.

title: When Is Your Child Ready for Orthodontic Treatment?
body: Prompted by growing client interest in orthodontics for kids, the post explains that the American Association of Orthodontists recommends an evaluation around age 7 -- not necessarily treatment at that age, but a good time to assess how existing and incoming teeth are developing.

Early treatment, called Phase 1, typically happens around age 8 or 9. At this stage it may be possible to correct bite problems, guide jaw growth, and create room for permanent teeth, which can reduce the odds of needing extractions later due to crowding.
The author's personal view is that early treatment isn't necessary for most patients, but can benefit children with more severe dental or skeletal conditions.

Signs suggesting a consultation may be worthwhile: noticeably crowded front teeth, protruding front teeth, early loss of baby teeth before age 5, teeth that don't meet properly, difficulty chewing or biting, a jaw that shifts when opening or closing the mouth, or thumb-sucking that continues past age 5.

Pine Smiles offers a free ongoing monitoring program that tracks young patients' growth to help determine the right time for treatment, if any -- with the goal of avoiding lengthier procedures, extractions, or surgery later on. Readers are invited to call Dr. Kim with questions.

title: Let's Talk About Oral Health During Pregnancy
body: Pregnancy brings physiological, dietary, and hormonal changes that raise the risk of gum disease and cavities. The post notes that unmanaged oral health problems during pregnancy can also increase the risk of cavities in the child, meaning a mother's oral care routine before, during, and after pregnancy affects her baby's future oral health.

It reassures readers that dental visits -- cleanings, exams, and asking questions about changes in the mouth -- are safe and important throughout pregnancy. X-rays are also safe as long as a lead apron covers the neck (protecting the thyroid) and belly.

Routine and urgent procedures like fillings and extractions can be done safely during pregnancy, and the post recommends treating them promptly rather than waiting, to avoid bacteria from dental problems entering the bloodstream.
One caveat: by the third trimester it becomes harder to lie flat for extended periods, so non-exam procedures (fillings, etc.) are best scheduled during the second trimester.

The overall message is that prenatal dental care benefits both the mother and, later, the child -- keeping infants and toddlers cavity-free from the start makes them less likely to develop cavities as they grow older.

title: Let's Talk About Parenting Styles
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post opens with a lighthearted nod to holiday visits from opinionated relatives, then runs through several well-known parenting-style categories, pairing each with a joking take on how that style might handle tooth-brushing resistance. It stresses there's no single right way to raise a child.
Authoritarian parenting is rule-driven and not open to negotiation ('because I said so'); the brushing joke is a strict two minutes, twice a day, no exceptions.

Authoritative parenting balances warmth with firmness and discusses rules as a family rather than simply imposing them; the brushing joke has everyone brushing together and learning from each other's technique.

Attachment parenting is rooted in staying physically close to a primary caregiver early in life and tends to avoid cry-it-out sleep training, with lots of communication; the brushing joke involves walking through the brushing 'plan' together like a rehearsal.

Permissive parenting is lenient, stepping in mainly for serious problems and acting more like a friend than an authority figure; the brushing joke is skipping brushing for the night if the child is tired.

Free-range parenting emphasizes independence appropriate to a child's ability and is said to build resilience; the brushing joke is that a child who finds a toothbrush in the woods will figure out how to use it.
The post closes by reassuring parents that as long as there are more smiles than scowls, they're doing a good job.

title: Children's Dental Health Month
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post walks through four pillars of pediatric dental care: brushing, flossing, fluoride, and sealants.

Brushing: start the habit as soon as kids wake up, ideally brushing alongside them so they can model the behavior. Use a soft-bristle brush; once a child can spit reliably, use a pea-sized amount of toothpaste, or a rice-grain-sized amount if they still swallow it. A consistent brushing pattern -- starting in the same spot and following the same order every time -- helps make sure every surface, including the gumline, gets covered.
Flossing: removes plaque and food between teeth that brushing alone can't reach, and helps with bad breath. The habit can be started even before a child's teeth are touching.

Fluoride: recommended in toothpaste from the start (not just once a child can spit), per the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry and the practice. A rice-grain amount is recommended for children two and under (safe if swallowed, though encouraging the child to let it drip out is best), moving to a pea-sized amount around age two. A fluoride application may also be recommended during cleanings. Parents can check their local water fluoridation levels through the CDC's My Water's Fluoride tool.

Sealants: molars are especially prone to cavities because their chewing surfaces have more pits and grooves that are harder for a toothbrush to clean, and because they do the most work chewing. The practice typically applies sealants around ages 6 and 12. The post cites a July 2017 Cochrane Collaboration report finding a 51% reduction in cavity prevalence among children whose teeth were sealed.

title: Let's Talk About Nutrition and Dental Health
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post explains why the practice shares nutrition content alongside dental advice, then breaks down several nutrients important for kids' health and where to find them.
Calcium supports strong bones and teeth, blood clotting, and muscle contraction; sources listed include oranges, tangerines, dried apricots, broccoli, kale, kiwi, dates, and plums.

Vitamin C helps repair tissue and build collagen (needed for ligaments, blood vessels, skin, and cartilage); sources listed include citrus fruit, strawberries, bell peppers, papaya, mango, brussels sprouts, and blueberries.
Iron is needed to make hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; sources listed include pumpkin, spinach, and broccoli.
Vitamin A supports vision, the immune system, the reproductive system, and heart, lung, and kidney function; sources listed include carrots, sweet potato, and winter squash.
Vitamin B2 helps convert fat, carbohydrates, and protein into usable energy; sources listed include spinach, soybeans, and asparagus.
Vitamin B3 supports skin, digestive, and nervous-system health and helps balance cholesterol; sources listed include tomato, avocado, and peas.
The post closes by hoping the information helps parents add at least one more fruit or vegetable to their family's routine.

title: Child Abuse Prevention Month
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post marks April as National Child Abuse Prevention Month, referencing a 2016 presidential proclamation from Barack Obama and noting that 2019's theme was 'Strong and Thriving Families,' symbolized by blue pinwheels.

The post frames child protection as a shared community responsibility and cites the World Health Organization's definition of child abuse as physical or emotional mistreatment, sexual abuse, neglect, or exploitation that harms a child's health, survival, development, or dignity within a relationship of trust or power.
It points readers to childwelfare.gov's 2019 Prevention Resource Guide and tip sheets, which cover topics such as tantrums, keeping families strong, financial stress, and building resilience in kids.

It lists six protective factors for families: nurturing and attachment, knowledge of parenting and child development, parental resilience, social connections, concrete support for families, and children's social and emotional competence.
The post closes with a call to commit to preventing abuse and neglect and to support all children in the community.

title: What's For Dinner?
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post opens by noting that good nutrition matters from the womb onward, while acknowledging that real family dinners rarely look like a nutrition ad.

It offers a downloadable weekly dinner-planning chart with 20 squares split across four food groups (fruit, vegetable, protein, carbohydrate), meant to be divided among family members so everyone gets to contribute favorite choices via sticky notes, then assembled into a week of balanced meals.

The post shares tips gathered from outside nutrition sources: involving kids in grocery shopping builds familiarity with food and useful life skills; avoiding comments on how much or what a child eats, since parents are responsible for offering balanced meals and kids for deciding how much to eat; avoiding labeling foods as 'good' or 'bad' and instead connecting foods to things kids care about, like protein for sports performance or a healthy breakfast for focus in class; and letting kids build their own plates from parent-provided options (protein, complex carbohydrate, vegetable, fruit, and a calcium source) to encourage them to try new foods through a sense of choice and autonomy.

title: Your Child's First Dental Visit
body: Answering a frequently asked question, the post explains that the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry recommends a first dental visit when a baby's first tooth erupts, or by their first birthday, whichever comes first -- though families who missed that window are welcome any time, including families new to the area.

It advises planning ahead by finding a pediatric dentist specifically, noting that pediatric dentists complete 2+ years of additional training beyond dental school in childhood growth and development, changes in a young child's mouth over time, and behavior management (essentially applied child psychology to help kids tolerate, and hopefully enjoy, visits). Pediatric dentists are also trained to treat children with special health care needs. The post suggests asking a pediatrician or friend for a referral, or searching the Diplomate directory at abpd.org for board-certified pediatric dentists.

It recommends completing intake forms in advance -- the practice emails a link that can be filled out on a phone or computer at home -- to streamline the visit, though forms can also be completed on-site if needed.

For the appointment itself, it suggests scheduling early in the day around naps and mealtimes, budgeting about an hour, bringing a list of medications, and bringing a second adult along if there are other children, so a parent can focus on the visit.

It lists common questions parents may want to ask during visits: whether the toothbrush being used is appropriate; whether the child should be using fluoride, fluoride toothpaste, or supplements; what snacks help keep teeth cavity-free; how to reach the dentist after hours in an emergency; what to do about thumb-sucking or pacifier habits; whether teeth are erupting properly and on schedule; and whether the child has a tongue or lip tie.

title: Protect Your Kids This Summer
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post rounds up summer-safety guidance from several outside sources, covering bug spray, sunscreen, sunglasses, goggles, hats, water bottles, and dental care.

Bug spray: citing the American Academy of Pediatrics, DEET-containing repellents are considered safe from two months of age; a higher DEET percentage means longer-lasting protection, not a stronger effect. DEET-free natural alternatives (citronella, lemongrass, peppermint, cedarwood oils) typically need more frequent reapplication. Repellent should go only on exposed skin and be rinsed off once indoors; DEET sprays don't expire.

Sunscreen: check that last year's bottles haven't expired, use broad-spectrum protection, apply 15-30 minutes before going outside, and reapply often, especially after swimming or sweating. Babies under six months should be kept in the shade rather than relying on sunscreen.

Sunglasses: look for lenses blocking 99-100% of UVA and UVB rays and meeting American National Standards Institute requirements (UV absorption up to 400 nanometers); letting kids pick a style they like makes them more likely to actually wear them.
Goggles: recommended for pool swimming, since public pools often lean toward over-chlorinating to stay sanitary, which can irritate eyes and skin; rinsing off right after swimming also helps.
Hats: add sun protection for the face, neck, and head; many schools ban hats in the classroom but allow them at recess, making recess a good time to build the habit.

Water bottles: encourage regular water breaks rather than waiting for thirst (which signals dehydration has already started); water-rich foods like grapes, watermelon, cucumber, and celery also help with hydration.

Dental care: don't forget twice-yearly visits, two minutes of brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, and flossing. The post notes that with the year half over, it's a good time to book a 2019 appointment if one hasn't happened yet.

title: Let's Talk About Dental Specialties
body: The post notes that pediatric dentists complete 2-3 extra years of training beyond dental school and make up roughly 5% of dentists in the US, then runs through the American Dental Association's ten recognized dental specialties.

Dental Anesthesiology is described as the newest specialty, recognized in 2019 -- dentists extensively trained in anesthesia who can work with other dentists to provide anesthesia in-office, avoiding a hospital or outpatient surgery center for children needing extensive treatment.
Dental Public Health specialists focus on improving oral health community-wide through prevention and health-promotion programs.
Endodontics covers root canal treatment.
Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology specialists identify and manage diseases affecting the mouth, including diagnosing biopsy samples.
Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology specialists focus on dental x-rays and imaging.
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery covers procedures like wisdom tooth removal; the practice refers many teenage patients out for this.
Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics covers braces and related care; pediatric dentists often refer patients to orthodontists at different growth stages.
Pediatric Dentistry is described as the only age-defined dental specialty, and the author's favorite.
Periodontics specialists focus on the health of gums and the bone supporting teeth.
Prosthodontics specialists restore and rebuild mouths using implants, dentures, crowns, and similar restorations.

title: Let's Talk About Tough Topics
body: Prompted by the approach of Stand Up to Cancer Day and September 11th, this post offers guidance on discussing difficult subjects with children.
It recommends not treating hard topics as taboo, staying matter-of-fact, and keeping emotional reactions in check so kids feel safe bringing up any subject without fear of a negative response.

Citing Dr. Lori Walsh via the Today Show, it suggests asking children what they already know and letting them explain it first, rather than launching straight into an explanation -- this avoids oversharing beyond what's age-appropriate and helps kids feel empowered.
It notes that children often piece together partial, sometimes distorted information from overheard news or conversations, so parents should gently correct misconceptions.
It advises keeping explanations simple and age-appropriate, avoiding graphic details or complex concepts that a young child isn't ready for.

To help kids feel safe, it suggests highlighting the people and systems working to keep everyone protected -- airport security, police, firefighters, and military, or, for health topics, reminding kids that regular doctor and dentist visits catch problems early.

It also suggests channeling concern into action, such as joining a cancer walk or writing letters to service members, and closes by encouraging parents to give kids time to process news and to remind them they can always come talk.

title: Let's Talk About Halloween 2020
body: Written for the first pandemic Halloween, this post links out to CDC guidance on staying healthy during the holidays and an Eater article covering safer Halloween ideas, then offers several lower-contact activity suggestions.
Photo scavenger hunt: teams (family members, or friends in their own neighborhoods) hunt for a shared list of spooky-themed photos ahead of October 31st.

Spooky-shape walk or run: using a mapping app like Map My Run, trace a route shaped like a ghost, bat, witch's hat, or jack-o-lantern, then compare route shapes with friends doing the same in their own neighborhoods.

Costumed Zoom dance party: a free Zoom account allows up to 100 participants for 40 minutes; the post suggests muting participants so everyone can hear their own music and building a shared costume-party playlist.

Reverse trick-or-treating: costumed kids stay in their own front yards while adults walk or drive around distributing treats -- described as a lower-risk alternative that requires some neighborhood coordination.
Whatever the activity, the post closes with a reminder to wear a mask, use hand sanitizer often, and wash hands upon returning home.

title: Let's Talk About How Dental Insurance Is Different From Health Insurance
body: This post, drawing on a WGBH history piece, explains why dental and health insurance developed as separate systems and behave differently today.

It traces health insurance back to 1929, when it was hospitals and physicians -- not insurance companies -- who first brought it to market in the US, through an early Blue Cross model where patients paid a small annual fee for a set number of covered hospital visits. The model spread quickly because it helped hospitals get paid reliably and helped patients budget for care, and it grew further during World War II.
Dental insurance came along much later -- the first plans weren't created until the 1950s, and they didn't become common until the 1970s.

The post explains that dental coverage functions more like a discount or membership program than true insurance: most plans cover routine services like cleanings at little or no cost up to an annual dollar cap, after which the patient covers everything themselves. Health insurance works in reverse, with costs increasingly covered by the insurer once a deductible is met, making dental plans much less like true risk-based insurance.
The post closes by encouraging patients to make full use of their dental benefits by scheduling exams and cleanings.

title: Let's Talk About Parenting Styles (February 2020)
body: This is a shorter, re-posted version of the practice's parenting-styles article, covering the same five categories -- Authoritarian, Authoritative, Attachment, Permissive, and Free Range -- with the same core descriptions as the November 2019 post but without the tooth-brushing jokes.

Note for the migration: this version's opening paragraph still contains unedited syndicated boilerplate referencing 'Charleston parents' and 'Magnolia Pediatric Dentistry' rather than Chino Hills or Pine Smiles -- it appears this post was published from a shared content template that wasn't fully localized. Flagging this rather than silently correcting it, since the instructions were to capture what's actually on the page.

Authoritarian parents enforce rules without much explanation or negotiation ('because I said so'). Authoritative parents balance firmness with warmth and discuss expectations as a family. Attachment parenting emphasizes staying physically close to a primary caregiver early on and tends to avoid cry-it-out sleep training. Permissive parents are lenient, stepping in mainly for serious problems and acting more like a friend than an authority figure. Free-range parents emphasize independence suited to a child's ability, which the post says can build resilience.
As in the earlier post, it closes by reassuring parents that more smiles than scowls means they're doing a great job.

title: Let's Talk About Respiratory Health
body: Published in late February 2020, this post addresses winter respiratory viruses and what was then called the 'Wuhan coronavirus (2019-nCoV).' Note for the migration: this content reflects the very early, fast-changing understanding of COVID-19 in February 2020 and reads as dated -- worth flagging to the client as a candidate to retire or replace rather than migrate as evergreen content.

General prevention tips given: plan ahead for possible disruptions, stock masks, gloves, hand sanitizer, and extra food to reduce trips out, disinfect door handles and surfaces, avoid handshakes, cough into an elbow, limit travel, and seek medical care if exposed.

The post describes 2019-nCoV as a betacoronavirus (like MERS and SARS) believed to have originated in bats via an animal source, with symptoms including fever, cough, and shortness of breath ranging from mild to severe or fatal. It cites the CDC's then-estimated incubation window of roughly 2 to 14 days and notes that infants, the elderly, pregnant women, and immunocompromised people were considered most at risk.

Recommended precautions: washing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds or using a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, avoiding touching the eyes, nose, and mouth, staying roughly six feet from anyone sick, staying home when sick, covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue and washing hands afterward, and disinfecting frequently touched surfaces. The post points readers to the CDC's Novel Coronavirus page for updates.

title: Let's Talk About the Dangers of Vaping
body: This post covers youth e-cigarette use in detail, opening with an August 30, 2019 CDC health advisory describing vaping as a public health crisis. It cites 2019 statistics that 27.5% of high school students had vaped in the past month, with close to 1 million youth vaping daily, e-cigarettes as the most-used tobacco product among teens, and 72% of youth users choosing flavored products. It lists product types and names including vape pens, e-cigars, e-hookahs, tanks, mods, personal vaporizers, and JUUL.

It explains that electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) are battery-powered devices with a heating element that vaporizes a solution for inhalation, first developed in China and marketed as a lower-harm alternative to, or even a cessation aid for, traditional cigarettes.

It emphasizes that nicotine is addictive and harmful to developing brains from the prenatal period through adolescence, and that many teens start vaping to fit in, often without considering it 'smoking.'

The post flags weak regulation compared to traditional tobacco: appealing flavors like chocolate, fruit, candy, bubblegum, mint, and pina colada (banned in regular cigarettes), free samples reaching underage users, and easy online ordering despite a legal purchase age of 18.

Because e-cigarette solutions aren't required to disclose ingredients, the post notes several health concerns found in vapor and solutions: propylene glycol as an eye/throat/airway irritant linked to asthma with long-term exposure, dangerously high nicotine concentrations in some products (with nicotine-poisoning symptoms including sweating, dizziness, vomiting, and rapid heart rate), and traces of nickel, lead, tin, acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, isoprene, and toluene.

It singles out JUUL as the most popular device among youth at the time, noting its pods carry higher and more concentrated nicotine than most competitors, that a large share of users reportedly didn't realize JUUL pods always contain nicotine, an FTC marketing investigation, and its ownership by Philip Morris.

Injury and poisoning statistics cited: 2,035 e-cigarette explosion/burn injuries treated in US emergency rooms from 2015-2017, more than 8,000 nicotine poisonings in children under 6 from 2012-2017, and, as of December 17, 2019, over 2,500 hospitalizations and 54 deaths across 27 states linked to e-cigarette use. The post points to AAPD, AAP, and HealthyChildren.org resources for further reading.

title: Let's Talk About Resources for Parents From the American Dental Association
body: This post highlights free public resources from the American Dental Association, an organization the post describes as having over 163,000 members and more than 160 years of history.
The ADA's Find-a-Dentist tool lets users search for ADA-member dentists by ZIP code and specialty, returning contact information and credentials.

MouthHealthy.org offers oral health guidance across life stages from pregnancy through adulthood, an ADA Seal of Acceptance product directory (a benchmark for product safety and efficacy, searchable by category or company), an A-Z topic index, nutrition guidance and holiday recipes, dental-visit FAQs, and downloadable activity sheets and lesson plans for kids.

The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD), with over 10,000 members, provides primary and specialty care for infants, children, adolescents, and patients with special health care needs. Its Oral Health Resources page links to dental and medical organizations, parenting sites, and federal and general health sites, and it offers free public access to its Reference Manual of Pediatric Dentistry.

The American Board of Pediatric Dentistry (ABPD) is the specialty's certifying board, maintaining a blog and a searchable directory of board-certified (Diplomate) pediatric dentists -- a credential the post frames as a sign of demonstrated, ongoing proficiency.

title: What's New in Pediatric Dentistry?
body: Published for National Children's Dental Health Month, this post shares updates attributed to the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry.

It notes that although overall tooth-decay prevalence has declined, nearly one in five children under age 5 has experienced dental decay, and recommends starting dental visits by a child's first birthday as the best prevention strategy.

It states that 15 million children in the US have special health care needs and face significant unmet dental care needs, and notes that pediatric dentists are specially trained to treat patients with special needs from childhood into adulthood.

The post frames tooth decay as affecting far more than teeth -- including mental health and self-esteem -- and argues that regular visits and early detection make care safer, more comfortable, and more affordable, citing a cost of up to $10,000 per child to treat severe decay, and up to $25,000 in the most severe cases. It also notes decay-related infections can spread to the ears, sinuses, and brain.
It states that the number of practicing dentists and pediatric dentists is projected to keep growing through 2030, outpacing growth in the child population.

The post highlights silver diamine fluoride as a growing, less invasive cavity treatment that can stop existing decay, harden softened areas of a tooth, reduce sensitivity, and help prevent further decay.

title: Let's Talk About Women in Dentistry
body: Published for International Women's Day, this post profiles several pioneering women in the history of dentistry.

Emeline Roberts Jones is described as the first woman to practice dentistry in the US. Her dentist husband initially disapproved, so she studied and practiced in secret; once he learned of her skill, he let her join his practice, and she eventually took it over after his death.

Vada Somerville is described as the second African American woman to earn a Doctor of Dental Surgery degree in California, at USC, and the first African American woman licensed to practice dentistry in the state. She pursued dentistry partly so she could keep her dentist husband's practice running if he were drafted during World War I, and was the only woman and only Black student in her class.

Jeanne Sinkford began studying at Howard University at age 16 and went on to become the first female dean of a US dental school. She received the ADA's Distinguished Service Award in 2015 and remains a dean and professor emeritus at Howard.

Lucy Hobbs Taylor is described as the first woman in the world to graduate from dental school. After being turned away from two Ohio dental schools, she trained under private tutors and practiced in Iowa without a formal degree, then enrolled as a senior once the Ohio College of Dentistry lifted its ban on women, becoming the first woman worldwide to earn a doctorate in dentistry.

Evangeline Jordan is credited as the first dentist to specialize in pediatric dentistry. She ran a dental clinic at a San Francisco orphanage while in school, later limited her Los Angeles practice to children, gave an influential 1916 talk connecting diet (less sugar, more milk, eggs, and vegetables) to children's dental health, and wrote the first pediatric dentistry textbook in 1925.
The post notes that despite repeated requests during both World Wars, women dentists were denied the chance to serve as military dentists and were only accepted as nurses.

Sara Krout, a Latvian immigrant with dental degrees from Latvia and the University of Illinois, became the first woman dentist in the US Navy in 1944 by joining the WAVES program, since military rules barred her from enlisting directly as a female dentist. She served at the Great Lakes Naval Training Station from 1944 to 1946 and remained in the Naval Reserve until 1961.

Ida Gray Nelson is described as the first African American woman to become a dentist in the US. Inspired by working for early women's-dentistry advocate Jonathan Taft, she worked her way through school as a seamstress, graduated from the University of Michigan School of Dentistry, and ran a practice serving both Black and white patients from 1890 to 1928, known for her gentleness with children.

Leonie von Meusebach-Zesch, born in Texas, served underserved populations throughout her career -- providing care to Civilian Conservation Corps workers and inmates at the California Institute for Women during the Depression, then practicing in Arizona (including patients from the Hopi and Navajo communities, using mobile equipment mounted on her car), and finally spending 15 years in the Alaska Territory, reaching remote villages by plane (surviving a crash) and by dog sled.

title: Let's Talk Going Off to College
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post offers a checklist for parents preparing to send a teen off to college.

Suggestions include: scheduling a dental cleaning around the school's break schedule; getting a pre-departure physical exam; filling prescription medications for the semester or setting up mail delivery to the new address; starting annual dermatology skin checks; and packing a first-aid kit with aspirin, antacids, vitamins, anti-diarrheal medicine, adhesive bandages, antibiotic ointment, and cough drops.
On move-in day, the post suggests locating fire and emergency exits and, for dorm residents, introducing the family to the resident advisor.

Other tips: visit the campus medical office together so the student knows where it is; walk the route to classes ahead of time to ease first-day nerves; find the on-campus counseling office and normalize having mixed feelings about the transition; find the tutoring center for academic support; and locate the nearest grocery store and a 24-hour pharmacy.

title: Let's Talk About Aerosols
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi during the early COVID-19 pandemic, this post explains what aerosols are and how they relate to dental office safety.

It defines an aerosol as a suspension of solid particles or liquid droplets in air, giving natural examples like mist, fog, clouds, wind-blown dust, sea salt, volcanic ash, and wildfire smoke, alongside human-made ones like air pollution, aerosol spray products, and even the fog from breath on a cold window.
It notes aerosols aren't inherently harmful -- they scatter light to create sunset colors and help seed clouds and rain, which in turn helps cleanse the atmosphere.

Particle size matters: larger droplets from a sneeze fall to the ground within about 3 to 6 feet, which the post ties to the CDC's six-foot social-distancing guidance, while smaller droplets can stay airborne and travel roughly 20 to 26 feet within seconds to minutes.

It notes the body has natural defenses against aerosols (like nasal hair and eyelashes), but these aren't enough against very small particles like the viruses behind COVID-19 or the flu, which is why hand hygiene matters so much.

The post describes changes made at the office to reduce aerosol exposure: staff wearing masks, goggles or face shields, and surgical caps; continued strict infection-control protocols and surface sanitizing between patients; removing toys from the waiting room; and limiting the number of family members accompanying each patient. It closes with a note that the team is still smiling under their masks and has missed seeing patients.

title: Let's Talk About Smiling Through Summer 2020
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post introduces a 'Bloom Where You're Planted' theme for the disrupted summer of 2020, promising further at-home activity ideas throughout the season.
It reminds readers to keep up social distancing, hand washing, and mask-wearing, and to watch local guidance on reopenings and closures even as restrictions ease.
For sun protection it recommends shade, protective clothing, and regular sunscreen use, drawing a parallel to routine oral-health habits.
It notes that staying hydrated supports saliva production, which helps wash away cavity-causing bacteria -- tying hydration directly to oral health.

For active play it recommends helmets for biking, scooting, and skateboarding, citing that helmets reduce the risk of head injury by about 50%, and suggests stocking a first-aid kit with kid-safe bug spray, antibacterial ointment, band-aids, and hydrogen peroxide for the inevitable summer scrapes.
It closes with the standard reminder to brush for two minutes twice daily, limit sugary snacks, and keep up six-month visits, noting the office remained open with added safety precautions in place.

title: Let's Talk About PIMU
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post introduces PIMU (Problematic Interactive Media Use), described as a relatively new DSM-5 diagnosis covering internet addiction, internet gaming disorder, gaming disorder, and media addiction -- an 'environmental condition of the digital age.'

It raises questions many parents have: how much screen time is appropriate, how to monitor apps and sites, how to tell when use has become a problem (for kids or for parents themselves), and where to find help.

It cites research suggesting media overuse can disrupt family life, school performance, and emotional, mental, and physical health, and explains that children and teens are especially vulnerable because the prefrontal cortex -- responsible for decision-making and judgment -- doesn't fully mature until the mid-twenties.

The post describes four ways PIMU can present clinically: excessive video gaming where a child resists stopping even when prompted; using social media as a primary substitute for in-person connection; obsessive pornography use leading to sexual dysfunction; and compulsive information- or video-seeking online that crowds out other activities.

Warning signs listed include social withdrawal, declining school performance, and reduced interest in personal hygiene. The post notes overlap with conditions like ADHD, social anxiety, depression, autism, and substance use, and potential links to eating disorders, weight gain, and sleep problems.

Recommendations include tracking how much, how often, and on how many devices each family member uses screens; aiming for a 'balanced diet of experiences'; using media mindfully; modeling good habits as a parent; and keeping screens out of bedrooms.

title: Back to School
body: Addressing the 2020 return to school -- in person, online, or a hybrid mix -- this post emphasizes open communication with kids about masks, distancing, and hand hygiene to ease anxiety about the pandemic.
It references Mayo Clinic guidance on mask types and effective use, stressing the importance of washing or sanitizing hands both before and after putting on or removing a mask.

It reminds readers that masks don't replace distancing, and suggests a hands-on way to teach kids what six feet looks like: measuring a familiar item, like a backpack, and figuring out how many backpack-lengths add up to six feet.

It stresses keeping hands and surfaces clean, including stocking classrooms with hand sanitizer and sanitizing wipes, and clarifies that the practice itself uses FDA-approved, ADA-recommended hospital-grade sanitizer rather than homemade wipes.

For home and school use, it shares a DIY surface-wipe recipe: cut a roll of paper towels in half with a serrated knife (VIVA brand is noted as cutting cleanly), place the half-roll in an airtight container, add 2 cups water, 1 cup rubbing alcohol (at least 70% concentration), 1 tablespoon dish soap, and optionally a few drops of essential oil, let the roll soak and flip it to saturate both ends, then remove the cardboard core so sheets can be pulled from the center.

title: Career in Dentistry
body: Aimed at kids who love science, this post pitches dentistry as a growing, in-demand career with room to specialize in areas like family practice, pediatric dentistry, or cosmetic dentistry.

It outlines several possible career paths: solo or partner private practice; academic dentistry, combining teaching, research, community service, and patient care; public health dentistry, which focuses on community prevention and promotion rather than private practice, including US Public Health Service roles on reservations, military bases, or in prisons; research careers working on advances like laser dentistry, bone-replacement implants, and computerized X-rays; international work through organizations such as the WHO, UNESCO, and the FAO, plus volunteer dental work in developing countries; and hospital dentistry, treating patients with medical conditions or disabilities alongside physicians.

It notes there are more than 60 dental schools in the US accredited by the ADA's Commission on Dental Accreditation, each evaluated for content and quality, with DDS/DMD programs taking four years to complete.

General prerequisite coursework is listed as roughly 8 semester hours each of biology with lab, physics, English, general chemistry with lab, and organic chemistry with lab, though specific requirements vary by school. The post also suggests summer internships at a dental practice as a way to explore the career firsthand.

title: Let's Talk About Saliva
body: Written by Dr. Avani Gandhi, this post takes a closer look at saliva -- also called spit, drool, slobber, spittle, or froth -- something every parent becomes very familiar with during teething.
It explains that saliva is produced by the salivary glands and contains minerals that help remineralize and harden teeth, including newly erupted baby teeth, which start out softer.
It notes that dry mouth, a common medication side effect, raises the risk of dental problems since saliva isn't cleansing the teeth as effectively, and recommends staying well-hydrated as a result.

Saliva's composition is described as water, mucus, proteins, mineral salts, and the digestive enzyme amylase, which begins breaking down complex carbohydrates; saliva also plays a role in speech and in the body's water balance.

The post details three major pairs of salivary glands: the sublingual glands under the tongue (producing mostly mucus through the Bartholin's ducts, responsible for the ability to 'gleek,' or squirt saliva), the submandibular glands under the jaw (via the Wharton's ducts), and the parotid glands, the largest, located between the ear and jaw (via the Stensen's ducts) -- plus several hundred minor salivary glands in the tongue, palate, lips, and cheeks.

It notes these glands produce one to two liters of saliva a day, most of which is swallowed, and that saliva lubricates the mouth, aids swallowing and digestion, and helps protect teeth by washing away food and bacteria.
